confounds: The diagnosed/control groups are highly imbalanced: 619 diagnosed users versus 5,463 controls.
Retained timeline volume differs by label, so raw post counts, token counts, unique-word counts, and unnormalized diversity measures can be misleading.
No timestamps or demographic metadata were available to separate observation duration, age, cohort, platform activity, or collection effects.
Simple lexical lists and punctuation rules are noisy for Portuguese slang, contractions, spelling variation, and polysemy.
Surface first-person markers do not reliably distinguish lived experience from quotation, lyrics, jokes, role-play, advocacy, news, or discussion of another person.
Punctuation-based sentence and clause proxies are sensitive to missing punctuation and social-media fragments.
Equal-user and pooled-post estimates can diverge substantially; prolific users should not dominate stylistic comparisons.

caveats: Pronoun and first-person verb markers are surface indicators and include possessives.
No full semantic attribution model was used to exclude quoted or performative language.
findings.evidence_summary: The strongest stylistic separation was a higher share of first-person-marked posts among diagnosed users, with a large and stable fold-wise gap.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use as a corpus-derived style feature, not evidence of lived experience; combine with persistence and context filters for quotation, lyrics, jokes, or role-play.

negative_results: Full-timeline lexical-diversity gaps were volume-sensitive: TTR was 0.328 versus 0.344 and entropy 6.094 versus 5.995, but after capping users at 500 tokens, TTR was 0.564 versus 0.560 and entropy 5.249 versus 5.229; several capped effects were not stable in fold 4.
Token-level negation frequency was not robust; one fold reversed, and pooled negation-bearing post frequency was nearly identical: 21.32% versus 21.18%.
Past- and future-tense marker rates were effectively null and inconsistent across folds.
Comma and quotation rates were weak or mixed; detected URLs, mentions, and hashtags were negligible or absent.
A modest third-person-post elevation was observed, but it does not distinguish first-person experience from discussion of others, advocacy, news, or narrative text.
